fields.title: What to count as a signal vs. noise
fields.keyTakeaway: A market news item becomes a signal only if you have written down in advance which of your decisions it can change. Without this, monitoring turns into reading a feed and reacting to the loudest noise.
fields.checkQuestion: A competitor announced a free plan. What is the first question you will ask yourself?
fields.blocks/0/text: Key node question: **what happened in the market that affects our plans?** Emphasis on the second half: most of what happens does not affect plans.
fields.blocks/1/text: **What happens if you do not answer the question.** Every news item about a competitor triggers a meeting. The team lives in reactive mode, and the roadmap gets rewritten based on Telegram posts.
fields.blocks/2/items/0: **Which of our decisions does this change?** If none, it is news, not a signal.
fields.blocks/2/items/1: **How sustainable is this?** A one-off promotion and a business model change require different things.
fields.blocks/2/items/2: **What will we see on our end if this matters?** Name a metric and timeframe — then in a month you will have something to check against.
fields.blocks/3/text:
First reaction in chat: "we need a free plan too".

Ran it through the filter. Decision it changes: entry price. Sustainability: the plan is limited to three documents per month — this is lead generation, not a model change. What we will see on our end: bounce rate on the pricing page and trial-to-paid conversion.

Agreed to do nothing and check those two metrics in a month. A month later, conversion had not changed: their free plan attracted those who needed a one-off document, and those are not Reestr clients.

A meeting saved, a quarter not rewritten.
fields.blocks/4/text: An opinion leader with a large audience might write about a product that solves a different problem for a different person. That is not your competitor, even if the wording overlaps.
fields.blocks/5/text: The filter protects against busywork but creates a risk of missing a real turning point: a regulatory shift, a payment provider exit, or the arrival of a player with a different model. That is why the filter should have exceptions — categories of events that are always evaluated, regardless of what you are doing right now.
